extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and scholars of psychology, literary/cultural history, and humour theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the conceptual dimensions and evaluative criteria used by Victorian and early-20th-century thinkers (Bain, Spencer, Sully, Ribot, etc.) for explaining laughter and humour, including physiological, social, and evolutionary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure linked to increase of vital functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Bain's physiological claim: pleasure was associated with an increase of 'the vital functions', while pain was associated with a decrease (The Senses and the Intellect, 1868).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that laughter fits because it represents a 'heightening of the powers of life' (1868: 291). Bain acknowledged exceptions and the vagueness of key terms; the account is offered as a general physiological principle rather than a precise mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degradation as the occasion of the ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Bain's reformulation of Hobbes: 'The occasion of the ludicrous is the Degradation of some person or interest possessing dignity, in circumstances that excite no other strong emotion' (1865: 248).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This replaces 'superiority' with a focus on degradation (targets: power, dignity, gravity). Examples include Pope's couplet about Queen Anne. Bain uses this to show that even 'genial humour' often contains an element of degradation disguised by compliments or geniality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release from constraint / rebound of hilarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bain's idea that laughter often accompanies a release from solemn posture or constraint: 'the rebound of hilarity ensues, as in the case of children set free from school' (1865: 250).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as physiologically linked to an increase of nervous energy; the release provides pleasure and can interact with degradation (mockery of dignity produces relief by releasing constraint). Used to explain why mockery provides momentary freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguised malevolent element in humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Bain's claim that even apparently innocent raillery contains a core element of degradation or malice: 'the indignity is disguised, and, as it were, oiled by some kindly infusion' (1865: 249).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He argues indignity is often disguised because overt degradation would be unacceptable to 'honest sympathy'; rhetorical means (compliment, genial tone) mask the aggression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining degradation with compliment to reduce indignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical technique: pairing a compliment with a degrading remark (de Quincey example on Kant measured 'by a carpenter') to soften the sting of degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bain cites this as a common device in 'genial humour' to veil malevolence and make ridicule socially palatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descending incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's key criterion: 'Laughter naturally results only when consciousness is unawares transferred from great things to small – only when there is what we may call a descending incongruity' (1864a: 116).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the goat interrupting a solemn theatrical reconciliation or Pope's bathos; Spencer argues only sudden 'descent' from sublime to petty produces the accumulated nervous energy that yields laughter. This refines incongruity theory by specifying directionality (great→small).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as purposeless muscular discharge regulating nervous energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's physiological account: laughter is a display of 'muscular excitement' that is purposeless in outward utility and functions to expend an 'overflow of nerve-force' (e.g., movements of chest, limbs; 1864a: 111).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts purposeful emotional actions (e.g., flight in fear) with purposeless laughter; explains laughter's bodily manifestations as an energy-dissipation mechanism rather than social communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Least Resistance (Spencer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's evolutionary-general law that nervous energy will be expended along channels which offer the least resistance; facial muscles are used first because they are frequently used and offer little resistance, producing inherited smiling/laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain how laughing responses become habitual and (per Spencer) transmitted through inheritance; ties physiological mechanism to an evolutionary account of the form and intensity of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all incongruities provoke laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation (Bain and Spencer): many incongruities do not produce laughter (e.g., 'a decrepit man under a heavy burden, five loaves and two fishes among a multitude ... an instrument out of tune, a fly in ointment, snow in May'), so incongruity alone is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates refinements (e.g., Spencer's 'descending' qualifier) and indicates contextual, affective, and physiological factors determine whether incongruity is laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns as interactional aggression / disruptive
rubrics_metrics.description: Norrick's empirical claim: puns produce 'interactional aggression in disrupting topical turn-by-turn talk' and set recipients tests of understanding (1993), functioning to disrupt conversational rules rather than merely amuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why puns can be experienced as aggressive; degradation may target conversational norms rather than specific individuals. Punning signals relief from rules while testing others, thus having both playful and adversarial qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbesian superiority theory (and its limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Older tradition (Hobbes): laughter arises from a sense of superiority. Bain and others critique this as incomplete—one need not feel personally superior to laugh at someone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bain reforms the idea toward 'degradation' rather than explicit superiority; later syntheses (Ribot, Sully) treat Hobbesian forms as 'lower' types of humour in an evolutionary schema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social functions of laughter (uniting and dividing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sully's claim that laughter is social in that it unites people ('laughter unites people') but also can be 'anti-social and dividing' when it laughs at others (1902: 255–6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that laughter both cements group bonds and enforces/reflects social hierarchies; laughter's social role can preserve existing inequalities (conservative function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrative/multidimensional approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Sully, Ribot, Dugas: no single theory covers all kinds of laughter; different theories (Hobbesian/degradation, incongruity, relief) each have limited domains and are best combined within an evolutionary or integrative framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend treating theories as complementary—e.g., Hobbesian as basic/low, incongruity as higher/developed, relief/physiological accounts explaining mechanism—rather than seeking a unitary explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental and evolutionary parallels (children and 'savage' laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sully's and Dugas's position that the laughter of children and of 'savages' (nineteenth-century phrasing) can mirror developmental stages and evolutionary progression from coarse to refined humour (1902: 228, 251).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to support evolutionary or developmental continuity: explosive, coarse forms in children/less 'developed' societies versus more sympathetic, complex humour in mature societies; note the historical/ideological bias in such characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spencer's physiological gradation of laughter intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's claim that the size of the descending incongruity determines the muscular reaction: small descent → smile (facial muscles), large descent → vocal laughter, body rocking, slapping sides (energy dissipation across more muscles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links the subjective comedic intensity to observable bodily reactions and the Law of Least Resistance; provides a graded physiological prediction about laughter's form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial-feedback influence on emotion (modern experimental support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention of modern experiments (Strack et al., 1988): using facial muscles involved in smiling (e.g., biting a pencil) can increase reported happiness, supporting the idea that bodily actions influence emotional experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited to suggest that bodily components of laughter/smiling can affect subjective feeling, aligning with or challenging aspects of James's and Spencer's positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as rebellion against order / mockery of hollow pretensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Bain's description that laughter delights in mocking 'hollow pretensions, affectation, assumption and self-importance, vanity, airs and coxcombry' and represents a 'rebellion against order' (1865: 251).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames humour as a socially subversive activity that releases constraint; yet the text notes that such apparent rebellion can function conservatively, reinforcing social norms by managing release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spencer's methodological focus on physiology over social explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's approach explains laughter via individual nervous-system mechanisms and evolutionary laws, explicitly avoiding social or communicative functions of laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to critiques that Spencer 'overlooks the social nature of laughter'—i.e., why laughter is typically shared and how it functions in social regulation remains unaddressed in his account.
